title: The Hebrew alphabet and its sounds
intro: The 22 letters, read from right to left, then the vowel marks and the small dots and signs that change how a word sounds. Sounds follow the pronunciation used in most colleges, based on Israeli Hebrew. Tap a letter for more, and Listen to hear an example.

letters.name: alef
letters.sound: silent: it carries a vowel
letters.tip: Say only its vowel: אָב is av.

letters.name: bet
letters.sound: b with the dot; v without
letters.tip: It has a little foot at the bottom right; כ (kaf) is rounded with none.

letters.name: gimel
letters.sound: g as in go

letters.name: dalet
letters.sound: d
letters.tip: A square corner at the top right; ר (resh) is rounded there.

letters.name: he
letters.sound: h; silent at the end of a word

example2.en: law: the final ה is silent

letters.tip: A gap at the top left; ח (chet) is closed.

letters.name: vav
letters.sound: v; also writes the vowels o (וֹ) and u (וּ)
letters.tip: A plain upright stroke; ז (zayin) has a cap.

letters.name: zayin
letters.sound: z

letters.name: chet
letters.sound: ch as in Scottish loch

letters.name: tet
letters.sound: t

letters.name: yod
letters.sound: y as in yes; also helps write the vowels i (ִי) and e (ֵי)
letters.tip: The smallest letter, hanging high: the “jot” of Matthew 5:18.

letters.name: kaf
letters.sound: k with the dot; kh without; ך at the end of a word

letters.name: lamed
letters.sound: l
letters.tip: The only letter that rises above the line.

letters.name: mem
letters.sound: m; ם at the end of a word

example.en: water: both forms in one word

letters.name: nun
letters.sound: n; ן at the end of a word

letters.name: samekh
letters.sound: s
letters.tip: Round all over; final ם is square.

letters.name: ayin
letters.sound: silent, as most people read today: it carries a vowel

letters.name: pe
letters.sound: p with the dot; f without; ף at the end of a word

letters.name: tsade
letters.sound: ts as in cats; ץ at the end of a word

letters.name: qof
letters.sound: k
letters.tip: Its tail drops below the line.

letters.name: resh
letters.sound: r

letters.name: shin, sin
letters.sound: sh with the dot on the right; s with the dot on the left

example2.en: field: dot on the left, s

letters.tip: The Ephraimites couldn't say sh, only s: “Shibboleth” (Judges 12:6).

letters.name: tav
letters.sound: t

sections.title: The vowels
body: Vowel marks sit under, over or beside a letter and are said after it. Here they are on ב (or on א where a vowel only goes with throat letters). They fall into three families: a, e/i and o/u.
Three small hateph vowels (ֲ ֱ ֳ) are quick versions of a, e and o, used under the throat letters א ה ח ע.

sections.title: Hear the vowels in real words
body: One word for each vowel, in the order of the table.

sections.title: Dots and marks that change the sound
body: A dot inside ב כ פ makes the sound hard: בּ b, כּ k, פּ p. Without it they are v, kh, f. (ג ד ת take the same dot, but it doesn't change their sound in this pronunciation.)
The same dot after a vowel doubles the letter: in הַשָּׁמַיִם the שּׁ counts twice. A dot in a final ה means it is sounded: לָהּ, “to her”, ends in h.
The dot on ש tells shin (שׁ, sh) from sin (שׂ, s). On ו it makes a vowel: וֹ is o, וּ is u; without it ו is the consonant v.
When ח or ע ends a word after another vowel, a patah is said just before it: רוּחַ is RU-ach. A shewa at the start of a syllable is said as a quick e; at the end of one it is silent.

examples.en: כּ k with the dot, final ף f without
the dot doubles שּׁ: the heavens
the dot in final הּ: to her
dot on the left: s, field
say the a before ח: spirit

sections.title: The throat letters
body: א ה ח ע (and often ר) are made at the back of the throat. They never take the doubling dot, and instead of a plain said shewa they take a hateph vowel (ֲ ֱ ֳ). They like a-vowels around them.
That is why “the” is הָ, not הַ, before them: הָאָרֶץ, the earth.

sections.title: Signs in the Bible text
body: ־ (maqqef) joins two words to be said as one: כָּל־הָאָרֶץ, kol ha-A-rets. ׃ (sof pasuq) ends a verse. ֑ (atnah), under a word, marks the middle of the verse.

Most words carry one of many small accent marks. They show the stressed syllable and work like punctuation (they were also a guide for chanting). You don't need to learn them all: just stress the syllable they mark.

A small ° in the Reader marks a word read differently from how it is written; tap it to see the written form. God's name יהוה is not said: readers say Adonai, “the Lord”, which is why English Bibles print LORD.
Two Hebrew letters sometimes stand alone between verses: פ and ס mark the end of a paragraph. The Reader uses them to start a new paragraph instead of printing them.

sections.title: How it sounded long ago
body: The pronunciation here is the one taught in most colleges, based on Israeli Hebrew. The scribes who added the vowel marks (the Masoretes) heard more differences: ו was w; ג ד ת without the dot were soft (gh, th as in this, th as in thin); ח and ע were throat sounds of their own; and ט ק צ were said further back than ת כ ס.
You don't need these to read, but they explain why Hebrew has two letters where we now hear one sound: ט and ת, כ and ק, ח and כ.

practice.say: be-re-SHIT ba-RA e-lo-HIM et ha-sha-MA-yim ve-ET ha-A-rets
practice.en: In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.

practice.say: she-MA yis-ra-EL a-do-NAI e-lo-HEI-nu a-do-NAI e-CHAD
practice.en: Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one.
The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.
